tool.name: jq
tool.tagline: Command-line JSON processor: query, filter and reshape JSON
tool.description: jq is a small, fast command-line program and language for slicing, filtering, transforming and generating JSON. It is the standard way to read API responses, cloud CLI output and JSON logs in shell scripts and pipelines.

glossary.def: A terminal program for reading, filtering and reshaping JSON data, e.g. jq '.name' user.json prints the name.
In jq, the instruction you give it saying what to output for each input, like .name or .[] | select(.age > 30).
jq's -r option: strings are printed as plain text, without the JSON double quotes around them.
In jq, an array of keys and positions that leads to one value inside a document, like ["user","tags",0].
The programming language that runs inside web pages in the browser. JSON's way of writing data comes from it.

concepts.name: What JSON looks like
concepts.summary: JSON writes data as text: objects in { } hold named values, arrays in [ ] hold lists, and values are strings, numbers, true/false or null.
concepts.why: jq exists to read and reshape JSON, so you need to recognise its few building blocks before anything else.
concepts.code:
# The same person written on one line, as programs usually send it:
echo '{"name":"Ann","age":31,"admin":true,"phone":null,"tags":["ops","oncall"],"address":{"city":"Oslo"}}' > ann.json

jq . ann.json      # jq lays it out readably (more in the next lesson)
# {
#   "name": "Ann",
#   "age": 31,
#   "admin": true,
#   "phone": null,
#   "tags": [
#     "ops",
#     "oncall"
#   ],
#   "address": {
#     "city": "Oslo"
#   }
# }
takeaways: { } is an object of "key": value pairs; [ ] is an array (a list)
A value is a string, number, true/false, null, object or array
Array positions (indexes) start at 0
pitfalls: Writing JSON by hand with single quotes or a comma after the last entry; both make it invalid.

quiz.q: In `{"tags": ["a", "b", "c"]}`, what is at index 1 of the tags array?
options: Nothing: positions start at 1, so index 1 is "a"
quiz.explain: Positions count from 0, so index 0 is "a" and index 1 is "b".

quiz.q: Which of these is valid JSON?
quiz.explain: JSON needs double quotes around keys and strings and no comma after the last entry.

concepts.name: Pretty-printing and field access
concepts.summary: jq '.' lays JSON out readably, .name pulls out one field, .a.b goes deeper and -r prints text without quotes.
concepts.why: Pulling one value out of a big chunk of JSON is the most common thing you'll ever do with jq.
concepts.body:
jq reads JSON from standard input, or from files you name, and runs a **filter** on it: a short instruction saying what to output. The simplest filter is `.`, the **identity**, which means "the whole input, unchanged". jq prints it neatly indented and coloured, which alone makes jq worth installing: `jq . data.json`, or `some-command | jq .` for output that arrives as one long line.

To pick fields:

- `.name` outputs the value of the key `name`.
- `.user.address.city` follows objects inside objects, one key at a time.
- `.["first name"]` or `."first name"` reaches keys with spaces or other unusual characters.
- A missing key gives `null`, not an error: `.nope` outputs `null`.

Strings come out as JSON, with their double quotes. Add `-r` (**raw output**) to print the bare text instead. That's what you want when saving a value in a shell variable: `name=$(jq -r .name user.json)`. The `$( )` runs the command inside it and puts what it printed into the variable.

If the input isn't an object, asking for a field is an error: `.name` on an array fails with "Cannot index array with name". Adding `?` hides the error and outputs nothing instead: `.name?`.

Always put the filter in **single quotes** in the shell. jq filters are full of characters the shell would otherwise treat specially, such as `|`, `[`, `$` and `"`.
concepts.code:
echo '{"user":{"name":"Ann","address":{"city":"Oslo"}},"first name":"A"}' > u.json
jq . u.json                    # pretty-printed and coloured
jq .user.name u.json           # "Ann"
jq -r .user.name u.json        # Ann
jq '.user.address.city' u.json # "Oslo"
jq '."first name"' u.json      # "A"
jq .user.phone u.json          # null
name=$(jq -r .user.name u.json); echo "hi $name"   # hi Ann
takeaways: jq . lays JSON out readably; .a.b pulls out nested fields
-r prints strings as plain text, without quotes
Single-quote jq filters in the shell
pitfalls: Forgetting -r when saving a value into a shell variable, so the variable holds the quote marks too.

quiz.q: What does `echo '{"a":{"b":1}}' | jq .a.c` print?
quiz.explain: Asking an object for a key it doesn't have gives null rather than an error.

concepts.name: Arrays: index, slice and iterate
concepts.summary: Pick array items with .[0], take a slice with .[2:4], and go through every item with .[] to get one output per item.
concepts.why: Almost every service returns lists, and .[] is how you handle each item in one.
concepts.body:
Array positions count from 0: `.[0]` is the first item, and `.[-1]` the last (negative numbers count from the end). A **slice** `.[2:4]` returns a smaller array, from index 2 up to but not including index 4; `.[:3]` takes the first three. Asking for a position that doesn't exist returns `null`.

`.[]` is the key idea of jq. It doesn't output an array: it outputs **each item separately**, one after another, as a stream of results. Whatever comes after it then runs once per item.

So `jq '.[].name'` prints the name of every object in a list, one per line.

`.[]` works on objects too, outputting each value. Combined with field access it digs through lists inside lists: `.orders[].items[].sku` gives the `sku` of every item of every order.

Because each item becomes a separate output, wrap the filter in square brackets to gather the results back into one array: `[.[].name]` gives `["Ann","Bob"]`. That pair, take apart then gather, is the basis of most jq work.

`length` counts the items of an array, the keys of an object or the characters of a string. `.[]?` goes through the items without an error when the input might not be an array or object.

Many tools write **JSON Lines**: one complete JSON value per line, common for logs. jq handles that directly, running the filter once for each value it reads.
concepts.code:
echo '[{"name":"Ann","tags":["a","b"]},{"name":"Bob","tags":["c"]}]' > p.json
jq '.[0].name' p.json         # "Ann"
jq '.[-1].name' p.json        # "Bob"
jq -r '.[].name' p.json       # Ann
                              # Bob
jq -c '[.[].name]' p.json     # ["Ann","Bob"]
jq -c '.[].tags[]' p.json     # "a"  "b"  "c"  (three outputs)
jq 'length' p.json            # 2
jq -c '.[0].tags[:1]' p.json  # ["a"]
takeaways: .[0], .[-1], .[a:b] pick one item or a range
.[] outputs each item as a separate result
Wrap in [ ... ] to gather results back into an array
pitfalls: Expecting .[] to return an array; it produces separate outputs, so wrap it in [ ] when you need a list.

quiz.q: Input `[1,2,3]`. How many separate outputs does `.[]` produce?
quiz.explain: .[] outputs each item as its own result: 1, then 2, then 3.

concepts.name: Pipes, commas and building JSON
concepts.summary: Chain filters with |, get several outputs with a comma, and build new objects and arrays with { } and [ ].
concepts.why: Reshaping data into exactly the fields you need is jq's everyday job.
concepts.body:
A jq filter is built from small filters joined by symbols. Two matter most:

- The **pipe** `a | b` works like the shell's pipe, but inside jq: every output of `a` is fed into `b`. `.users[] | .email` is the same as `.users[].email`, but a pipe lets you put any filter in between.
- The **comma** `a, b` runs both filters on the same input and outputs the results of both: `.name, .age`.

Curly braces build a new object:

- `{name: .user.name, id: .user.id}` makes an object with those two keys; each value is a filter run on the input.
- Shorthand: `{name, id}` means `{name: .name, id: .id}`.
- A key worked out from the data goes in parentheses: `{(.key): .value}`.
- If a value gives several outputs, you get several objects, which can surprise you.

Square brackets `[ ... ]` collect every output of the filter inside them into one array: `[.items[].price]`.

Putting it together, `.users[] | {name, email: .contact.email}` turns a long, detailed reply into a short list of objects, one per user. Add `-c` (compact) to print each on one line, handy for passing to other commands such as `grep`.

Parentheses group things as you'd expect. Without them, `|` is applied last: `.a, .b | f` means `(.a, .b) | f`.
takeaways: a | b feeds each output of a into b
a, b gives the outputs of both
{name, id: .x} builds objects; [ ... ] collects outputs into an array
pitfalls: Writing {name: .tags[]} and getting one object per tag; a value with several outputs multiplies the objects.

quiz.q: What does `jq -c '{a: (1,2)}' <<< 'null'` output?
quiz.explain: Each output of the value expression produces a separate object.

concepts.name: Filtering with select and map
concepts.summary: Keep only matching items with select(condition), change every item with map(f), and compare with ==, <, and, or, not.
concepts.why: Filtering a list down to what you care about, like failed jobs or large files, is the core of most jq one-liners.
concepts.body:
`select(cond)` outputs its input **if** the condition is true, and nothing otherwise. Used after `.[]`, it filters the items:

`.[] | select(.status == "failed")`

Conditions compare with `==` (equal), `!=` (not equal), `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=`, and combine with `and`, `or` and `not`. `not` is a filter, so it comes after a pipe: `.done | not`.

Values that count as true in a condition are called **truthy**, and those that count as false **falsy**. In jq only `false` and `null` are falsy; `0`, `""` and `[]` all count as true.

`map(f)` runs `f` on every item of an array and returns a new array. It is exactly `[.[] | f]`. So these two are the same way to filter an array while keeping it an array:

- `map(select(.price > 100))`
- `[.[] | select(.price > 100)]`

Useful tests inside `select`: `has("key")`, `.name | startswith("tmp")`, `test("^err")` for a regular expression, and `IN(...)` to check against a list of values: `select(.env | IN("prod","staging"))`.

`map_values(f)` does the same as `map` for an object's values. Note that `select` drops inputs that don't match, so `map(select(...))` can make an array shorter, while `map(.price * 2)` keeps one result per item.
concepts.code:
cat > jobs.json <<'EOF'
[{"id":1,"status":"ok","ms":120},{"id":2,"status":"failed","ms":900},
 {"id":3,"status":"failed","ms":40},{"id":4,"status":"ok","ms":3000}]
EOF
jq -c '.[] | select(.status == "failed") | .id' jobs.json   # 2  3
jq -c 'map(select(.ms > 500) | .id)' jobs.json              # [2,4]
jq -c 'map(select(.status == "ok" and .ms < 1000))' jobs.json
# [{"id":1,"status":"ok","ms":120}]
jq -c 'map(.ms * 2)' jobs.json                              # [240,1800,80,6000]
jq -c '[.[] | select(.id | IN(1,4)) | .id]' jobs.json        # [1,4]
jq 'map(select(.status != "ok")) | length' jobs.json        # 2
takeaways: select(cond) lets its input through only when cond is true
map(f) = [.[] | f]; map(select(...)) filters an array
Only false and null are falsy in jq
pitfalls: Using select on a whole array (select(.x) on [...]) instead of on its items; use .[] or map first.

quiz.q: Which filter returns an array of only the items whose price is above 10?
quiz.explain: map applies select to each element and collects the survivors into a new array.

quiz.q: What does `[0, 1, null, false, ""] | map(select(.))` return?
quiz.explain: select(.) keeps truthy items; in jq only false and null are falsy, so 0 and "" stay.

concepts.name: Command-line options and passing variables
concepts.summary: Use -r, -c, -n, -s and -e, and pass shell values safely into a filter with --arg, --argjson and $ENV.
concepts.why: Scripts need clean output, correct exit codes and a safe way to pass shell values into a filter, never by pasting them into the filter text.
concepts.body:
The options you'll use constantly:

- `-r` prints strings without quotes, `-c` puts each output on one line, `-j` is like `-r` but adds no line break after each output.
- `-n` (null input) runs the filter once with `null` as its input instead of reading anything, used to **create** JSON from scratch.
- `-s` (slurp) reads all inputs into **one array**, e.g. to sort or count the records of a JSON Lines file.
- `-e` sets the exit code from the last output: 1 if it was `false` or `null`, 0 otherwise. Great for `if jq -e '.ready' status.json; then ...`.
- `-S` sorts object keys; `--tab` and `--indent n` control the layout.
- `-R` reads lines of plain text as strings; `-Rs` reads the whole input as one string.

**Passing values in.** Never build the filter by pasting a shell variable into it, like `"select(.name == \"$name\")"`. A quote in the value breaks the filter, and a value crafted on purpose could change what the filter does; that's called an **injection attack**. Instead:

- `--arg name "$value"` defines `$name` inside jq as a **string**.
- `--argjson n 5` reads the value as JSON, so it can be a number, an object and so on.
- `--slurpfile x file.json` loads a file's values as an array in `$x`.
- `$ENV.HOME` or `env.HOME` reads environment variables.
- `--args` after the filter makes the remaining arguments available in `$ARGS.positional`.

Combine `-n` with `--arg` to build JSON safely for other tools, such as the data curl sends to a web service.
concepts.code:
echo '[{"name":"Ann","age":31},{"name":"Bob","age":25}]' > p.json
n="Ann"
jq --arg n "$n" '.[] | select(.name == $n) | .age' p.json   # 31
jq --argjson min 30 -c 'map(select(.age >= $min))' p.json    # [{"name":"Ann","age":31}]
jq -n --arg user "$USER" --argjson admin true '{user: $user, admin: $admin}' -c
# {"user":"alice","admin":true}
printf '{"v":1}\n{"v":2}\n' | jq -s 'map(.v) | add'        # 3
printf 'a\nb\n' | jq -R -c '[., length]'                  # ["a",1] ["b",1]
echo '{"ready":false}' | jq -e .ready >/dev/null; echo $?  # 1
jq -n '$ENV.HOME'                                          # "/home/alice"
takeaways: -r raw, -c compact, -n no input, -s slurp, -e exit code
--arg (string) and --argjson (JSON) pass values in safely
-n with --arg builds JSON for other tools
pitfalls: Splicing shell variables into the filter text instead of using --arg.

quiz.q: `count=5` in the shell. Which passes it as a number to jq?
quiz.explain: --argjson parses the value as JSON, giving the number 5; --arg would give the string "5".

quiz.q: What does `-s` do with three JSON objects, one per line, on standard input?
options: Reads them into a single array of three objects
Processes them one at a time
quiz.explain: Slurp collects all inputs into one array, so the filter runs once.

concepts.name: Strings, regex and output formats
concepts.summary: Put values into text with "\(.x)", split, join and match text with regular expressions, and output CSV, TSV or shell-safe text with @csv, @tsv, @sh.
concepts.why: Turning JSON into text other tools read, such as spreadsheet files, log lines or shell arguments, is a classic jq job.
concepts.body:
**String interpolation** puts values into text: `"\(.name) is \(.age)"`. Any filter works inside `\( )`, and values that aren't strings are turned into their JSON text.

jq has many built-in **functions**: named filters, some taking arguments in parentheses, separated by `;`. For text:

- `split(", ")` and `join("-")` convert between a string and an array of pieces; `ascii_downcase`, `ascii_upcase`, `ltrimstr("v")`, `rtrimstr(".json")`, `startswith`, `endswith`.
- `tostring` and `tonumber` convert; `length` counts characters.
- Regular expressions (jq uses the Oniguruma engine, much like Perl's): `test("^err"; "i")` returns true or false (`"i"` ignores case), `capture("(?<user>\\w+)@(?<host>.+)")` returns an object of the named groups, `sub(re; repl)` and `gsub` replace, `scan(re)` outputs every match. Backslashes must be doubled inside jq strings.

**Format strings** turn data into text safely:

- `@csv` and `@tsv` turn an **array** into one line of **CSV** (comma-separated values, the plain-text table that spreadsheets open) or TSV (the same with tabs), with correct quoting. Use them with `-r`.
- `@sh` quotes values for use as shell arguments, and `@uri` applies **URL encoding** (a space becomes `%20`).
- `@base64` and `@base64d` convert to and from **base64**, a way to write any data using only letters, digits and a few symbols. `@html` and `@json` escape text for those formats.
- A format can also go before a string: `@uri "https://x.io/q?s=\(.term)"` encodes only the parts filled in.

A typical report: `jq -r '.[] | [.id, .name, .email] | @csv'` produces a CSV file you can open in a spreadsheet.
concepts.code:
echo '[{"id":1,"name":"Ann Lee","email":"ann@x.io"},{"id":2,"name":"Bob, Jr","email":"BOB@X.IO"}]' > u.json
jq -r '.[] | "\(.id): \(.name)"' u.json                 # 1: Ann Lee   2: Bob, Jr
jq -r '.[] | [.id, .name, .email] | @csv' u.json         # 1,"Ann Lee","ann@x.io"
                                                         # 2,"Bob, Jr","BOB@X.IO"
jq -c '.[] | .email | ascii_downcase | capture("(?<user>[^@]+)@(?<host>.+)")' u.json
# {"user":"ann","host":"x.io"}  {"user":"bob","host":"x.io"}
jq -c 'map(.name | split(" ") | .[0])' u.json            # ["Ann","Bob,"]
jq -r '.[] | select(.email | test("x\\.io$"; "i")) | .id' u.json   # 1  2
jq -r '@uri "https://s.io/?q=\(.[0].name)"' u.json       # https://s.io/?q=Ann%20Lee
takeaways: "\(expr)" interpolates values into strings
test, capture, sub, gsub, split, join for text work
@csv/@tsv on arrays, @sh, @uri, @base64 for safe output
pitfalls: Using @csv on an object or a string; it needs an array, so build one with [ ... ] first.

quiz.q: Which produces a correctly quoted CSV row from fields id and name?
quiz.explain: @csv takes an array and handles quoting of strings containing commas or quotes.

concepts.name: Working with objects: keys, entries, merge
concepts.summary: List keys, rename and filter keys with with_entries, delete fields with del, and merge objects with + and *.
concepts.why: Cleaning, renaming and combining objects is everyday work on settings files and on data from web services.
concepts.body:
Basic object functions:

- `keys` returns the key names, sorted (`keys_unsorted` keeps the input order); `has("k")` tests for a key; `length` counts keys.
- `del(.password, .internal)` removes keys; `pick(.a, .b.c)` (1.7+) keeps only the given fields, even nested ones.
- `to_entries` turns `{"a":1}` into `[{"key":"a","value":1}]`, and `from_entries` turns it back.
- `with_entries(f)` is `to_entries | map(f) | from_entries`: the standard way to **rename**, **filter** or **change keys**.

Examples: `with_entries(select(.value != null))` drops null fields; `with_entries(.key |= ascii_upcase)` uppercases the keys (`|=` updates a value in place, covered later); `with_entries(select(.key | startswith("_") | not))` drops keys starting with `_`.

**Merging**: `+` merges two objects; for a key in both, the right side wins. It only looks at the top level. `*` merges **recursively**: objects inside objects are merged too, at every depth. That's perfect for laying your own settings over a set of defaults. `add` on an array of objects merges them all with `+`.

To combine two files, read both and merge: `jq -s '.[0] * .[1]' defaults.json overrides.json`.

Output keeps the keys in their input order, but most functions that list keys sort them. Add `-S` to sort every output's keys, so comparing two outputs line by line shows only real changes.
takeaways: keys, has, del, pick for inspecting and trimming
with_entries(f) renames or filters keys through {key, value}
+ merges the top level (right wins), * merges at every depth
pitfalls: Using + to lay nested settings over defaults and losing the other keys inside; use * to merge at every depth.

quiz.explain: * merges nested objects recursively; + would replace .a entirely.

concepts.name: Sorting, grouping and aggregating
concepts.summary: Summarise arrays with sort_by, group_by, unique_by, min_by, max_by, add and length.
concepts.why: Quick counts, totals and top-N lists from JSON data answer many questions without a spreadsheet or a script.
concepts.body:
jq can summarise data on its own: counts, totals, averages. Combining many values into one summary is called **aggregation**. These functions all work on **arrays**, so start from an array, or gather separate outputs first with `[...]` or `-s`.

- `sort` and `sort_by(.field)` put items in order; `sort_by(.a, .b)` sorts by several keys; `reverse` flips the result for largest-first.
- `group_by(.field)` sorts and splits the array into an array of groups, each an array of the items that share that value.
- `unique` and `unique_by(.field)` remove duplicates (and sort).
- `min_by(.f)` / `max_by(.f)` return the item with the smallest / largest value; `min` / `max` work on plain values.
- `add` sums numbers, joins strings or arrays end to end, and merges objects. `add / length` is the average.
- `length` counts; `first`, `last` and `limit(n; f)` take parts.

The classic count-per-value pattern:

`group_by(.status) | map({status: .[0].status, count: length})`

It gives one object per status. To get a single object keyed by status instead, build entries: `map({key: .[0].status, value: length}) | from_entries`.

Top N: `sort_by(.ms) | reverse | .[:3]`. For JSON Lines logs, slurp them first: `jq -s 'group_by(.level) | map({level: .[0].level, n: length})' app.log`.
concepts.code:
cat > s.json <<'EOF'
[{"svc":"api","status":"ok","ms":120},{"svc":"web","status":"err","ms":900},
 {"svc":"api","status":"err","ms":40},{"svc":"api","status":"ok","ms":300}]
EOF
jq -c 'group_by(.status) | map({status: .[0].status, count: length})' s.json
# [{"status":"err","count":2},{"status":"ok","count":2}]
jq -c 'group_by(.svc) | map({key: .[0].svc, value: (map(.ms) | add / length)}) | from_entries' s.json
# {"api":153.33333333333334,"web":900}
jq -c 'sort_by(.ms) | reverse | .[:2] | map(.ms)' s.json     # [900,300]
jq -c 'max_by(.ms) | .svc' s.json                            # "web"
jq -c 'map(.svc) | unique' s.json                            # ["api","web"]
jq 'map(.ms) | add' s.json                                   # 1360
takeaways: sort_by, group_by, unique_by, min_by/max_by work on arrays
group_by(.k) | map({k: .[0].k, n: length}) counts per value
add sums; add / length averages
pitfalls: Calling group_by on separate outputs (.[] | group_by...) instead of on the array itself.

quiz.q: What does `group_by(.t)` return for `[{"t":"a"},{"t":"b"},{"t":"a"}]`?
quiz.explain: group_by returns an array of groups, each an array of the items sharing the value, sorted by that value.

concepts.name: Conditionals, defaults and error handling
concepts.summary: Branch with if-then-elif-else-end, supply defaults with //, and handle bad input with try, catch and the ? operator.
concepts.why: Real-world JSON is messy: missing fields, nulls and values of the wrong kind need graceful handling.
concepts.body:
**if** needs an `else` before jq 1.7 (since 1.7 it may be left out and defaults to `.`): `if .ms > 1000 then "slow" elif .ms > 200 then "ok" else "fast" end`. Like everything in jq, `if` produces a value, so it can sit inside object construction.

The **alternative operator** `a // b` outputs `a` unless it gives only `false` or `null` (or nothing at all), in which case it outputs `b`. It's the usual way to supply a default: `.name // "unknown"`, `.tags // []`. Careful: `false // true` is `true`, so it's no good for defaulting true/false values that may really be false; use `if .flag == null then true else .flag end` there.

**Errors**: asking the wrong kind of value for something (`.foo` on a string), `tonumber` on `"abc"` and an explicit `error("msg")` all raise errors that stop jq with exit code 5. Catching them so the program carries on is called **exception handling**:

- `try expr` swallows errors, producing no output for that input.
- `try expr catch handler` runs the handler with the error message as its input: `try tonumber catch "bad: \(.)"`.
- `expr?` is shorthand for `try expr`: `.[] | .id?` skips items that aren't objects.

Combine them to tidy sloppy data: `(.port | tonumber?) // 80` turns a string like `"8080"` into a number, or falls back to 80.
concepts.code:
echo '[{"ms":1500},{"ms":300},{"ms":20},{"name":"x"}]' > t.json
jq -c 'map(if .ms == null then "n/a" elif .ms > 1000 then "slow" elif .ms > 200 then "ok" else "fast" end)' t.json
# ["slow","ok","fast","n/a"]
jq -c 'map(.name // "unknown")' t.json        # ["unknown","unknown","unknown","x"]
echo '["8080","abc",null]' | jq -c 'map((tonumber? // 80))'   # [8080,80,80]
echo '"abc"' | jq 'try tonumber catch "bad input"'       # "bad input"
echo '[1,{"id":2},"x"]' | jq -c '[.[] | .id?]'           # [2]
echo 'false' | jq '. // true'                            # true  (beware!)
echo '{}' | jq 'error("missing id")'; echo "exit $?"     # jq: error ... exit 5
takeaways: if/elif/else/end is an expression
a // b defaults when a is null, false or empty
try/catch and ? handle errors per value
pitfalls: Using // to default booleans: a real false value is replaced by the default.

quiz.q: What does `{"enabled": false} | .enabled // true` return?
quiz.explain: // treats false like null, so the alternative true is returned.

quiz.q: What does `[.[] | .id?]` do with an element that is a string?
quiz.explain: .id? catches the indexing error and produces no output for that element.

concepts.name: Variables, reduce and defining functions
concepts.summary: Bind values with as $x, fold a stream with reduce, and define your own reusable functions with def.
concepts.why: Bigger transformations, like combining two lists or building lookup tables, need variables, running totals and helpers.
concepts.body:
**Variables**: `expr as $x | body` runs `body` with `$x` set to each output of `expr`. It's how you keep an outer value while going deeper: `.team as $t | .members[] | {team: $t, name}`. You can also unpack an object into several variables at once: `. as {name: $n, tags: [$first]} | ...`.

**reduce** boils a stream of values down to one, like keeping a running total on paper: `reduce .[] as $item (init; update)`. It starts from `init` and runs `update` once per item. Inside `update`, `.` is the running value so far (often called the accumulator).

- Sum: `reduce .[] as $x (0; . + $x)`.
- Build a lookup object: `reduce .[] as $u ({}; .[$u.id | tostring] = $u.name)`.

`foreach` is similar but outputs every in-between value, useful for running totals.

**Your own functions** are defined with `def name: body;`, or with **parameters** (named inputs) as `def name(f): body;`. Parameters are **filters**, not values: `def twice(f): f | f;`. Put `$` before a parameter to receive a value instead: `def add_tax($rate): . * (1 + $rate);`. A function may call itself (**recursion**), and functions can be kept in a file loaded with `-L dir` plus `import "name" as n;` or `include`.

A powerful pattern combines these to match two lists, such as orders to users. `INDEX(.users[]; .id)` builds an object of users keyed by id; then each order looks up its user: `INDEX(.users[]; .id) as $u | .orders[] | .user = $u[.user_id | tostring].name`.
concepts.code:
echo '[3,5,7]' | jq 'reduce .[] as $x (0; . + $x)'          # 15
echo '[1,2,3]' | jq -c '[foreach .[] as $x (0; . + $x)]'    # [1,3,6] running total
echo '{"team":"core","members":[{"name":"Ann"},{"name":"Bob"}]}' |
  jq -c '.team as $t | .members[] | {team: $t, name}'
# {"team":"core","name":"Ann"}  {"team":"core","name":"Bob"}
echo '[100,250]' | jq -c 'def add_tax($r): . * (1 + $r); map(add_tax(0.25))'   # [125,312.5]
echo '[1,2]' | jq -c 'def twice(f): f | f; map(twice(. * 10))'                 # [100,200]
cat > d.json <<'EOF'
{"users":[{"id":1,"name":"Ann"},{"id":2,"name":"Bob"}],"orders":[{"oid":7,"user_id":2}]}
EOF
jq -c 'INDEX(.users[]; .id) as $u | .orders[] | .user = $u[.user_id | tostring].name' d.json
# {"oid":7,"user_id":2,"user":"Bob"}
takeaways: expr as $x | body binds variables
reduce .[] as $x (init; update) folds a stream
def f(g): ...; takes filters; def f($v): takes values
pitfalls: Expecting a function parameter without $ to be a value; it is a filter evaluated against the current input.

quiz.q: What does `reduce .[] as $x (1; . * $x)` return for `[2,3,4]`?
quiz.explain: Starting from 1, the accumulator is multiplied by each element: 1*2*3*4 = 24.

concepts.name: Updating JSON: |=, +=, del and in-place edits
concepts.summary: Modify parts of a document while keeping the rest with update-assignment |=, arithmetic updates like +=, and plain = for setting values.
concepts.why: Editing settings files, bumping version numbers and changing data before passing it on all need one field changed without rebuilding the whole document.
concepts.body:
Most jq filters **pull out** data. Assignment operators instead return the **whole input** with something changed.

- `.version = "2.0"` sets a field, creating it if missing. The right side is evaluated against the **original input**, so `.b = .a` copies `.a` into `.b`.
- `.price |= . * 1.1` **updates**: the right side runs with the **current value at that place** as its input. This is the one you want most of the time.
- Arithmetic shortcuts: `.count += 1`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=`, and `//=`, which sets a default only if the value is null or false.

The left side can be any filter that points at places in the input, including `.[]` and `select`:

- `.items[].price |= . * 0.9` discounts every item.
- `(.items[] | select(.sku == "A1") | .qty) += 5` updates only matching items.
- `.users |= map(select(.active))` filters a list inside the document.

`del(...)` removes, with the same kind of left side: `del(.items[] | select(.sku == "B2"))`.

jq never edits files in place. Write to a temporary file and move it over the original: `jq '.version = "2.0"' package.json > tmp && mv tmp package.json` (or use the `sponge` command from the moreutils package). Writing with `>` straight to the file you read (`> package.json`) empties it before jq reads it, leaving nothing.
concepts.code:
echo '{"version":"1.0","items":[{"sku":"A1","qty":1,"price":10},{"sku":"B2","qty":3,"price":20}]}' > o.json
jq -c '.version = "2.0" | .version' o.json                     # "2.0"
jq -c '.items[].price |= . * 0.5 | [.items[].price]' o.json    # [5,10]
jq -c '(.items[] | select(.sku == "A1") | .qty) += 5 | .items[0].qty' o.json   # 6
jq -c '.items |= map(select(.qty > 1)) | .items | length' o.json   # 1
jq -c '.owner //= "nobody" | .owner' o.json                     # "nobody"
jq -c 'del(.items[] | select(.sku == "B2")) | .items' o.json
# [{"sku":"A1","qty":1,"price":10}]
jq '.version = "2.0"' o.json > o.tmp && mv o.tmp o.json        # safe "in-place" edit
takeaways: |= updates with the value at the path as input; = uses the whole input
Left side can use .[] and select to update many places
Write to a temp file then mv; never > the same file
pitfalls: Running jq ... file.json > file.json, which empties the file before jq reads it.

quiz.explain: |= updates .a using its current value (1) as input, and returns the whole object.

quiz.q: Input `{"a":1,"b":5}`. What is `.a = .b`?
quiz.explain: With plain =, the right side is evaluated against the whole input, so .b is 5.

concepts.name: Recursion and paths: .., paths, walk
concepts.summary: Search entire documents with .. and paths, read and write by path with getpath/setpath, and transform every node with walk.
concepts.why: Deeply nested JSON with no fixed shape, like Kubernetes or Terraform files, needs tools that work at any depth.
concepts.body:
`..` (recurse) outputs the input and **every value nested inside it**, going all the way down one branch before the next. It answers "find X anywhere": `.. | .image? // empty` lists every `image` field however deep, and `.. | numbers` every number. (`?` and `// empty` skip values that aren't objects, and nulls.)

A **path** is an array of keys and indexes leading to one value, like `["spec","containers",0,"image"]`.

- `paths` outputs the path of every value; `paths(type == "number")` keeps only paths whose value passes a test; `leaf_paths` is `paths(scalars)`: paths to single values such as numbers and strings, not objects or arrays.
- `path(expr)` gives the paths an expression would touch: `path(..|select(type=="string" and test("secret")))`.
- `getpath(p)`, `setpath(p; v)` and `delpaths([p...])` read and write by path array. With `reduce` they allow changes that work on any document.
- `to_entries` works on one level; `paths` works on all of them.

`walk(f)` applies `f` to every value **from the innermost outwards**, rebuilding the document: `walk(if type == "object" then del(.managedFields) else . end)` removes a key everywhere, and `walk(if type == "string" then ascii_downcase else . end)` lowercases every string.

Combining them, you can flatten a document into dotted keys: `[paths(scalars) as $p | {key: $p | map(tostring) | join("."), value: getpath($p)}] | from_entries`. This is invaluable for comparing two large settings files.
concepts.code:
cat > k.json <<'EOF'
{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"app","image":"app:1.2"},{"name":"log","image":"fluent:2"}],
 "meta":{"managedFields":[1],"labels":{"tier":"Web"}}}}
EOF
jq -c '[.. | .image? // empty]' k.json                        # ["app:1.2","fluent:2"]
jq -c '[paths(type == "string")] | .[0]' k.json               # ["spec","containers",0,"name"]
jq -c 'getpath(["spec","meta","labels","tier"])' k.json       # "Web"
jq -c 'setpath(["spec","replicas"]; 3) | .spec.replicas' k.json   # 3
jq -c 'walk(if type == "object" then del(.managedFields) else . end) | .spec.meta' k.json
# {"labels":{"tier":"Web"}}
jq -c '[paths(scalars) as $p | {key: ($p | map(tostring) | join(".")), value: getpath($p)}]
       | from_entries | keys[:2]' k.json
# ["spec.containers.0.image","spec.containers.0.name"]
takeaways: .. visits every nested value; combine with ? and // empty
paths, getpath, setpath, delpaths work with path arrays
walk(f) changes every value, innermost first
pitfalls: Using .. | .field without ?, which errors as soon as it reaches an array or a single value such as a number.

quiz.q: Which removes every `managedFields` key at any depth?
options: walk(if type == "object" then del(.managedFields) else . end)
quiz.explain: walk visits every node, deleting the key from each object; del(.managedFields) only touches the top level.

concepts.name: Large inputs: inputs, --stream and limits
concepts.summary: Process huge files and endless streams with -n and inputs, the --stream event format, and early-exit helpers like first and limit.
concepts.why: jq normally holds each JSON value fully in memory; files of many gigabytes and endless log streams need different techniques.
concepts.body:
By default jq reads each top-level JSON value completely into memory before running the filter. For JSON Lines that's fine: each line is small and handled on its own. Trouble starts with one **huge** value, such as a 5 GB array, or when you need to keep track of something across many records.

**inputs**: with `-n`, the filter starts with `null` and calls `input` (the next value) or `inputs` (all remaining values, read one at a time only as needed). `jq -n 'reduce inputs as $r (0; . + $r.bytes)' access.log` sums a field across millions of lines **without** gathering them into one array, unlike `-s`, which holds everything in memory.

**--stream** reads the document bit by bit and outputs **events**: `[path, leaf]` for every single value (a leaf: a string, number, true/false or null), plus closing markers `[path]`. Memory stays small however big the document is.

- `fromstream(...)` rebuilds values from events, and `1 | truncate_stream(inputs)` removes the first step of every path. So `jq -cn --stream 'fromstream(1 | truncate_stream(inputs))' big.json` outputs each item of a giant top-level array one at a time.

**Stopping early** saves time: `first(f)`, `limit(n; f)`, `until` and `input` stop after what they need. `jq -n 'first(inputs | select(.level == "error"))' app.log` stops at the first error.

Also useful: `--seq` for the JSON text sequence format (RFC 7464), which puts a separator character before each value; `input_filename` to know which file a value came from; and `$__loc__`, which gives the file and line of your filter, for tracking down problems.
concepts.code:
printf '{"bytes":10}\n{"bytes":32}\n{"bytes":8}\n' > access.log
jq -n 'reduce inputs as $r (0; . + $r.bytes)' access.log     # 50  (constant memory)
jq -n '[limit(2; inputs | .bytes)]' -c access.log            # [10,32]
jq -n 'first(inputs | select(.bytes > 20))' -c access.log    # {"bytes":32}

echo '[{"id":1},{"id":2}]' > big.json
jq -c --stream . big.json
# [[0,"id"],1]  [[0,"id"]]  [[1,"id"],2]  [[1,"id"]]  [[1]]
jq -cn --stream 'fromstream(1 | truncate_stream(inputs))' big.json
# {"id":1}
# {"id":2}
jq -r 'input_filename' access.log big.json | uniq           # access.log  big.json
takeaways: -n with inputs reads records one at a time, unlike -s
--stream outputs [path, leaf] events for huge single documents
fromstream(1 | truncate_stream(inputs)) splits a giant array
pitfalls: Using -s on a log of several gigabytes just to count or sum; reduce over inputs instead.

quiz.q: Why is `jq -n 'reduce inputs as $x (0; .+1)'` better than `jq -s 'length'` for a huge JSON Lines file?
options: It never holds all records in memory at once
quiz.explain: inputs reads values one by one, while -s builds a single array of everything first.

concepts.name: Generators, backtracking and empty
concepts.summary: Every jq expression can produce zero, one or many outputs; that explains surprise combinations, empty, and label/break.
concepts.why: Every 'why did I get four results?' or 'why did nothing print?' puzzle in jq comes from its generator semantics.
concepts.body:
Every jq expression is a **generator**: for one input it can produce **zero, one or many** outputs. `.[]` produces many, `select` zero or one, `empty` **none**, and `,` puts the outputs of two expressions one after the other.

When an operator such as `+` combines two expressions that each give several outputs, jq evaluates **every combination** of them:

- `(1,2) + (10,20)` outputs four values: `11, 12, 21, 22` (the right side changes in the outer loop).
- `{a: (1,2), b: (3,4)}` produces four objects.
- `[.[] | .x] | length` is safe, but `.[].x + .[].y` combines every x with every y, a common accidental blow-up.

`empty` is useful: in `if cond then . else empty end` it removes the value, and `select(f)` is defined as exactly `if f then . else empty end`. A function that produces `empty` inside `[...]` simply adds nothing.

Under the hood jq **backtracks**: after passing one output on to the rest of the filter, it goes back to the generator for its next one. `limit(n; f)` and `first(f)` stop a generator early using `label $out | ... break $out`, which you can use yourself to leave a loop.

`range(n)`, `range(from; upto; by)`, `recurse(f)`, `repeat` and `until(cond; next)` are the building blocks for generators. For loops that carry a running value, prefer `reduce` or `foreach` over deeply recursive `def` functions: they use a fixed amount of memory however long they run.
takeaways: Expressions produce zero, one or many outputs
Operators with two sides evaluate every combination of their outputs
empty produces nothing; label/break and limit stop generators early
pitfalls: Combining two .[] expressions in one arithmetic or object expression and getting N x M results.

quiz.q: How many outputs does `(1,2,3) * (1,2)` produce?
quiz.explain: Every combination of the 3 left and 2 right outputs is evaluated: 6 results.

quiz.q: What does `[1, empty, 2]` evaluate to?
quiz.explain: empty produces no output, so it contributes nothing to the array.
